title: Darwin’s abominable mystery
teaches: How quickly flowering plants spread, how their family tree is read from DNA and why it overturned some groupings by looks, Amborella, and telling monocots from eudicots

blocks.text: In July 1879, three years before he died, Charles Darwin wrote to his friend Joseph Hooker, director of Kew Gardens: "The rapid development as far as we can judge of all the higher plants within recent geological times is an abominable mystery." By the higher plants he meant the flowering plants, and the mystery was in the rocks. In layers from the age of the dinosaurs, flowering plants seemed to appear suddenly and already varied, with no long line of ancestors beneath them.

For a theory of slow change by selection this was awkward. Darwin wondered whether flowering plants had evolved for a long time somewhere that left no fossils, a lost island or continent, before spreading over the world.[^ball] He didn't settle it, and it is still not fully settled. But a great deal has been learned since, about when they spread and, from DNA, about how they are related.

The oldest fossils that are surely flowering plants are pollen grains about 135 million years old, from the early part of the Cretaceous period, the last age of the dinosaurs, which ran from about 145 to 66 million years ago. Lesson 17's land plants had been on land for more than 300 million years by then, and conifers, cycads and ferns ruled the forests. Small flowers, a few millimetres across, turn up in rocks from Portugal and elsewhere from about 125 million years ago, preserved as charcoal by ancient fires, and from the same age in China comes *Archaefructus*, a water plant with its seeds in small pods along the stem.

Then they spread fast. By about 100 million years ago flowering plants were common on every continent, and by the end of the Cretaceous, 66 million years ago, they made up most of the kinds of plant in many places. Today there are about 300,000 kinds of flowering plant, against about 600 conifers. Why they spread so fast is still argued. Animal pollinators (lesson 18) help, and so does double fertilisation, which stocks a seed with food only once it has been fertilised. So does speed: many flowering plants go from seed to seed in months, where a conifer takes years.[^small]

For two centuries botanists grouped plants by how they looked: the number and arrangement of flower parts, the shape of leaves, the kind of fruit. Linnaeus's first system counted stamens (branch K's first lesson). Later systems weighed many features together, but all of them had to decide which resemblances meant shared ancestry and which were coincidence, and that was a matter of judgement.

DNA gave a way to count. Each kind of plant carries copies of the same genes, slowly changed by mutation since their common ancestor. Mutations build up at a roughly steady rate and mostly without changing how the plant looks, so the more two kinds differ, the longer ago they split. In 1993 Mark Chase and 41 colleagues compared one gene[^rbcl] across almost 500 kinds of seed plant, and drew the first big family tree of the flowering plants from DNA. Much of the old grouping survived. Some of it didn't.

blocks.caption: Eleven flowering plants grouped by looks, and by DNA.
blocks.task: Guess, then switch to the DNA tree

guess.ask: The sacred lotus has round leaves floating on ponds and big many-petalled flowers, like a water lily. Which is its closest living relative?

views.label: By looks
views.title: Grouped by looks
views.text: Grouped by how they look, the lotus sits with the water lilies: round leaves floating on ponds and big many-petalled flowers. Switch to the tree read from DNA.

views.label: From DNA
views.title: Read from DNA
views.text: The lotus’s closest relatives are the plane trees and the proteas. Its floating leaves and big flowers are a way of life it shares with water lilies, arrived at separately. Amborella branches off first, and the water lilies next.

blocks.text: The sacred lotus, with its floating leaves and big pink flowers, had always been put with the water lilies. Its DNA put it beside the plane trees, the big trees with peeling bark that line city streets, and the proteas of South Africa. Living in ponds had given the lotus and the water lilies a similar look, arrived at separately, in the way that sharks and dolphins share a shape. The DNA trees also put together the plants that the cabbage white of lesson 20 eats: cabbages, capers and nasturtiums sit on one branch, with their shared mustard oils.[^apg]

The DNA trees answered another question: which living flowering plant is on the branch that split off first from all the rest? In 1999 several teams, comparing different genes, found the same answer. It is *Amborella trichopoda*, a straggly shrub with small cream flowers that grows only in the damp mountain forests of New Caledonia, an island in the South Pacific. It is the only species on its branch.

Amborella is not the ancestor of the other flowering plants. It has been evolving for as long as they have. But its line split off first, so a feature it shares with conifers and ferns was probably present in the first flowering plants too, and lost later on the other branches. Its wood has no wide water pipes, only the narrow cells of conifers and ferns, which suggests the earliest flowering plants had none either. Its flowers are separate too: each plant is usually either male or female. The water lilies split off next, then a few small groups, then the magnolias and their relatives. Nearly everything else falls into two great branches, the monocots and the eudicots.

parts.title: Monocots and eudicots in your hand

blocks.text: The **monocots**, about one flowering plant in five, include grasses and the cereals, lilies, onions, palms, bananas and orchids. The **eudicots**, about three in four, include beans, roses, oaks, cabbages, tomatoes and sunflowers. Both names refer to the seed leaves (cotyledons): a monocot seedling comes up with one, and "eudicot" means "true dicot", with two. Both branches were recognised long before DNA, and DNA confirmed them, with a tidy-up: a few two-seed-leaved plants, such as the water lilies and magnolias, turned out to belong to older branches of their own.[^grooves]

blocks.caption: A monocot and a eudicot: four things to look at.

blocks.text: Each feature has exceptions, but together they rarely mislead. A grass blade or a tulip leaf has long parallel veins; an oak or a bean leaf has a branching net. A tulip, a lily or an iris has its flower parts in threes or sixes. A buttercup, a rose and an apple blossom have five petals, and a wallflower or a poppy four.

blocks.title: Estimate
points: Think of ten flowers you know and sort them by threes against fours and fives. Tulip, lily, iris, daffodil and crocus come in threes or sixes; rose, buttercup, apple, geranium and poppy in fours or fives.
Among all flowering plants about one in five is a monocot. Garden lists like this one run high, because bulbs such as tulips and daffodils are popular.

blocks.text: Collect five leaves on a walk, from grass, a tree, a garden weed, a lily or iris if there is one, and anything else, and sort them by their veins. Then hold a flower and count its petals.

This is where the trunk of the course ends. The branch on keys and families takes this further: how Linnaeus named every plant with two words, how to use a key to name a plant you don't know, the ten families that make up most of what you will meet, and the look-alikes that will poison you if you mix them up.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the flowering-plant tree
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

choices: Flowering plants appear suddenly and already varied in the fossil record
Their flowers are too soft to fossilise
Flowering plants appear before any other land plants
items.why: In Cretaceous rocks they seemed to appear abruptly with no line of ancestors, which was awkward for gradual evolution.

items.ask: From DNA, the sacred lotus's closest relatives are the plane trees and proteas, not the water lilies. Why did it look like a water lily?
choices: Living in ponds shaped both in similar ways, separately
It is descended from water lilies
DNA tests on lotus were mixed up with water lily samples
items.why: Similar ways of life can produce similar looks in unrelated plants. Resemblance is not always shared ancestry.

items.ask: What does it mean that Amborella's line split off first from all other flowering plants?
choices: Its line split off first from the line that led to all the others
It is the ancestor of all other flowering plants
It is the oldest living plant
items.why: It is a cousin, not an ancestor: it has evolved as long as the others. But its early split makes it a guide to their common ancestor.

items.ask: A plant in a damp meadow has long blade-like leaves and blue star-shaped flowers of six parts. What is it most likely to be?
items.why: Parallel veins and parts in threes or sixes mark a monocot, such as a lily or a tulip.

items.ask: Which of these is a eudicot?
items.why: A bean comes up with two seed leaves and has net-veined leaves. Wheat (a grass) and onions (with parts in threes) are monocots.

items.ask: Why can't plants be grouped reliably by looks alone?
choices: Unrelated plants can come to look alike, and relatives can come to look different
Looks only mislead for water plants
items.why: Looks evolve with way of life. DNA, whose changes build up steadily and mostly regardless of looks, is a better record of who split from whom.

summary: **Darwin called the flowering plants' sudden appearance an abominable mystery (1879).** They seem to arrive in the Cretaceous with no long line of ancestors.
**The oldest sure flowering-plant fossils are about 135 million years old.** By 66 million years ago they made up most of the kinds of plant in many places.
**Their family tree is now read from DNA.** Chase and 41 colleagues drew the first big one in 1993.
**Looks can mislead.** The sacred lotus is closest to plane trees and proteas, not water lilies.
**Amborella's line split off first.** A shrub from New Caledonia, it is a cousin of all other flowering plants, not their ancestor.
**Most flowering plants are monocots or eudicots.** Monocots: one seed leaf, parallel veins, parts in threes. Eudicots: two seed leaves, net veins, parts in fours or fives.

small.title: Smaller cells
small.text: One recent idea is that flowering plants were able to shrink their genomes, which let them build smaller cells, which let them pack more veins and pores into each leaf and photosynthesise faster than the conifers and ferns around them. It is one suggestion among several, and the reasons probably add up.

apg.title: The Angiosperm Phylogeny Group
apg.text: Since 1998 a group of botanists calling itself the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group has published a classification of flowering-plant orders and families based on the DNA trees, revised in 2003, 2009 and 2016. Most botanical gardens and floras now follow it, which is why some plants have moved family in newer field guides.

grooves.title: Three grooves
grooves.text: The eudicots are defined by a feature you need a microscope to see: their pollen grains have three grooves or pores, where the pollen tube can come out. Monocots, water lilies and magnolias have one. Botanists had noticed this before DNA, and the DNA trees showed that the three-grooved plants form one branch.

ball.title: Darwin's lost continent
ball.text: Darwin had just read a lecture by the Irish botanist John Ball, who thought flowering plants had evolved on high mountains. Darwin disagreed in his letter to Hooker and floated instead "some isolated island, or whole continent, now sunk in the sea", perhaps toward the South Pole, where they could have developed out of reach of the fossil beds we know.

rbcl.title: The chloroplast gene
rbcl.text: The gene was *rbcL*, which sits in the chloroplast, the green body inside a plant cell that carries a small ring of DNA of its own. It encodes half of RuBisCO, the enzyme that grabs carbon dioxide from the air in photosynthesis. Every green plant has it, and because the job barely allows mistakes, the gene changes slowly enough to compare across all seed plants.
